cards.name: Pop-art colour halftone
cards.summary: A photo or illustration is rebuilt from big overlapping cyan, magenta, yellow and black dots on rotated screens, the enlarged-print rosette of pop art.
use_for: bold social backgrounds from a plain photo
avoid: small output sizes with a large radius: the image dissolves into dots; scale the radius to the print size
faces you need to recognise at a glance: keep the original underneath at partial opacity
files going to a real CMYK press: the simulated dots clash with the press screen (moire); flatten to a high resolution and proof

steps.note: Layer > Duplicate Layer: ran, 'Background copy' sits above the original, which stays untouched, and is active.
Image > Adjustments > Brightness/Contrast on the copy: Brightness +10, Contrast +40, non-legacy. Ran; a punchier base for the dots.

Filter > Pixelate > Color Halftone on the copy: Radius 12 px, screen angles 108 / 162 / 90 / 45. Ran. The run shows overlapping cyan, magenta, yellow and black dots with a rosette pattern across the whole picture, the pop-art look. At 12 px fine detail dissolves into dots; keep the original under it at partial opacity so the people stay recognisable (untested), and use a radius of 20 or more for large posters.

history: Brightness/Contrast; active layer: Background copy
history: Color Halftone; active layer: Background copy

verified.note: Whole frame rebuilt from large overlapping cyan, magenta, yellow and black dots on rotated screens with a visible rosette; at Radius 12 the subjects are hard to read, as the recipe warns.

steps.note: On the placed image or the artwork group: Effect > Pixelate > Color Halftone, same angles. Illustrator runs Photoshop Effects as raster effects at Document Raster Effects Settings resolution: set 300 ppi for print first.

Halftone (Color Transform) with Max dot radius 10: the call sends the angles KAngle 45, CAngle 15, MAngle 75, YAngle 0 and MaxRadius 10. Run: the page changed by 63.17 on average (0-255). The photo is a coarse coloured dot screen. The photo is already a bitmap, so the recipe's Convert to Bitmap step is not needed.
ApplyBitmapEffect('HalftoneEffect KAngle=45,CAngle=15,MAngle=75,YAngle=0,MaxRadius=10')

verified.note: The photo is rebuilt as a coarse overlapping cyan, magenta, yellow and black dot screen across the whole frame, colour bars included; the pop-art rosette reads clearly.

cards.name: Newsprint mono halftone
cards.summary: A photo printed like an old newspaper: one black dot screen whose dots grow with the shadows, on a warm off-white paper tone with a little ink speckle.
use_for: background photos that must stay quiet behind type
avoid: fine detail you need to read: a coarse screen erases it
shrinking the result afterwards: resampled dots turn to grey mush or moire; build it at final size
the Photoshop Bitmap route on an RGB document: Image > Mode > Bitmap only works on Grayscale

steps.note: Image > Mode > Grayscale: ran, the colour channels become one Gray channel (the plan works on the open document, not a copy).

Image > Mode > Bitmap (script, replaces the separate BitmapConversionOptions step): changeMode(BITMAP) with a BitmapConversionOptions of method HALFTONESCREEN, resolution 72 ppi, 9 lines per inch, angle 45, round dots. The recipe's 20 to 35 lpi assumes a 300 ppi output; the test plate is 72 ppi, so the frequency is scaled to give 8 px cells. The first attempt failed on a misspelt enum (the DOM name is BitmapHalfToneType). Ran.
steps.script:
var o = new BitmapConversionOptions(); o.method = BitmapConversionType.HALFTONESCREEN; o.resolution = 72; o.frequency = 9; o.angle = 45; o.shape = BitmapHalfToneType.ROUND;
d.changeMode(ChangeMode.BITMAP, o);

steps.note: Back to Grayscale, then RGB (script: two changeMode calls): ran, so a coloured paper tone can be added above.
steps.script: d.changeMode(ChangeMode.GRAYSCALE); d.changeMode(ChangeMode.RGB);

steps.name: Add Noise

Script (new last step): a solid #F3EBD8 fill layer on top set to Multiply, the paper tone. Ran. The run shows one black dot screen whose dots grow in the shadows on a warm off-white tone, an old-newspaper print. The picture is 1920 px wide at 72 ppi: build it at the final size, as the recipe says, since resizing turns the dots to mush.

cards.name: Risograph two-ink print
cards.summary: Two flat fluorescent inks (typically pink and blue) printed as grainy halftones that overlap into a third colour and sit slightly out of register.
use_for: indie posters, zines and event flyers
a warm, imperfect alternative to full colour
avoid: brand colours that must match exactly: riso inks and offsets are approximate by design
more than two or three inks: the look turns muddy
large solid areas of both inks: they overprint dark; give each ink its own parts of the image

steps.note: Layer > New > Layer from Background (new first step): ran, 'Layer 0' labelled 'ink1', needed for the layer styles below.
Layer > Duplicate Layer on ink 1 (target 'ink1'): ran, 'Layer 0 copy' (labelled 'ink2') is active. The bottom layer is ink 1, the top ink 2.

steps.name: Desaturate
steps.note: Image > Adjustments > Desaturate on ink 2 (target 'ink2'): ran, greyscale.

steps.name: Desaturate
steps.note: Image > Adjustments > Desaturate on ink 1 (new step, target 'ink1'): ran, greyscale.
Filter > Sketch > Halftone Pattern on ink 1 (target 'ink1'): Size 3, Contrast 12, Dot. Ran; a black-and-white dot screen.
Filter > Sketch > Stamp on ink 2 (target 'ink2'): Light/Dark Balance 20, Smoothness 6. Ran; flat black-and-white shapes.

steps.name: Color Overlay
steps.note: Layer Style > Color Overlay on ink 2 (new step, target 'ink2'): Screen, #3C78FF (a lighter ink blue than the first run's #0078BF, so the overprint with pink comes out violet rather than near-black navy), 100 %. Ran; black turns blue.

Without it the Multiply below does not overprint: a Screen colour overlay on a layer set to Multiply blends with what is under it, so in the first run the blue shapes knocked the pink out (blue areas measured pure ink blue). Ran.

Ink 1 set to Multiply (target 'ink1'): ran.

Ink 2 set to Multiply (new step, target 'ink2'): ran. The run now shows the blue shapes multiplying with the pink dot screen under them: where both inks print the colour is a deep blue-violet (about RGB 76 / 50 / 223 over the dark areas, against ink blue 60 / 120 / 255 and ink pink 255 / 72 / 176), where only pink prints it is pink.

Script on ink 2 (target 'ink2'): translate(6, 4) for the misregistration. The recipe's 3, 2 px was hard to see at 960 px; 6, 4 px shows as a thin offset fringe of pure blue along the right and lower edges of the blue shapes against the pink. Ran.

The first judge's knock-out (blue areas pure ink blue) is fixed.

steps.note: Edit Colors > Recolor with Preset > Two Color on the artwork, mapping it onto the two ink colours (menu path only: no executeMenuCommand id is known).
Put each ink's objects on its own layer and set them to Multiply so overlaps darken like ink.
On the second ink's group: move 1.5 pt right and 1 pt down, no copies: the misregistration (vertical sign unconfirmed).
Effect > Texture > Grain on each ink group for the print texture. Illustrator runs Photoshop Effects as raster effects at Document Raster Effects Settings resolution: set 300 ppi for print first.

steps.script:
a = s.Duplicate(0, 0)
b = s.Duplicate(0, 0)
labels["inkA"] = a
labels["inkB"] = b
result = a
steps.note: Setup (script): two copies of the photo, one for each ink (a riso job prints each ink from its own black-and-white separation).
Desaturate on the first separation: grey tones.
Light effect: contrast +10, brightness +15: the pink separation prints the shadows and the middle tones.
Halftone on the first separation: max dot radius 5, black screen at 45 degrees: a coarse dot screen, the grain of the pink ink.
Desaturate on the second separation.
Light effect: contrast +35, brightness +45: the blue separation only prints the deepest shadows, so the two inks take different shares of the tones.
Halftone on the second separation: the black screen at 75 degrees, the usual second screen angle, so the dots of the two inks cross.

steps.script:
def ink(src, hexcol, dx, dy):
    r = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
    r.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb(hexcol))
    r.Outline.SetNoOutline()
    r.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
    r.Transparency.MergeMode = 11
    sr = app.CreateShapeRange()
    sr.Add(src)
    sr.Add(r)
    bmp = sr.Group().ConvertToBitmapEx(4, False, False, 96)
    bmp.Move(dx, dy)
    return bmp

a = ink(labels["inkA"], "#FF48B0", 0.0, 0.0)
b = ink(labels["inkB"], "#0078BF", 0.14, -0.1)
b.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
b.Transparency.MergeMode = 9
paper = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
paper.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#FBF1DE"))
paper.Outline.SetNoOutline()
paper.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
paper.Transparency.MergeMode = 9
labels["inkA"], labels["inkB"] = a, b
result = b
steps.note: Inks and register (script): each separation gets a flat ink colour: a rectangle of fluorescent pink (#FF48B0) or blue (#0078BF) in If Lighter mode over the grey dot screen turns the dark dots into the ink colour on white, and the group is flattened to a bitmap. The blue separation is then moved 0.14 in right and 0.1 in down (the misregistration) and set to Multiply over the pink one, so the overlap prints dark violet; a warm paper tone (#FBF1DE, Multiply) goes on top.
script ran
ApplyBitmapEffect('DesaturateEffect ')
ApplyBitmapEffect('SMHEffect Intensity=0,Highlights=0,Shadows=0,Midtones=0,Contrast=10,Brightness=15')
ApplyBitmapEffect('HalftoneEffect CAngle=15,MAngle=75,YAngle=0,KAngle=45,MaxRadius=5')
ApplyBitmapEffect('DesaturateEffect ')
ApplyBitmapEffect('SMHEffect Intensity=0,Highlights=0,Shadows=0,Midtones=0,Contrast=35,Brightness=45')
ApplyBitmapEffect('HalftoneEffect CAngle=15,MAngle=75,YAngle=0,KAngle=75,MaxRadius=5')
script ran

verified.note: Improved: a coarse dot screen in pink and navy with a visible offset at the frame edges and on the strip text. But the blue ink never prints on its own (about 1% of pixels) and bare paper almost never shows (under 1%), so it reads as pink plus a dark overlap rather than two inks; the colour halftone also leaves green and yellow specks (about 13% of pixels) that belong to neither ink.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW: pick the two inks and shape their curves in the Duotone dialog.
Illustrator: decide which objects print in which ink (the Two Color recolour mapping) by eye.

cards.name: Screen-print flat colour
cards.summary: An image reduced to a handful of flat ink colours with simplified, slightly rough shapes, like a hand-pulled screen print or gig poster.
use_for: T-shirt and merch artwork (limited ink count)
avoid: subtle gradients and skin tones you need to keep: they band into flat steps
type inside the image: the simplification breaks small letters into shards; set type on top afterwards
real screen-print separations from the Photoshop result alone: trace to vector so each ink is a clean shape

steps.note: Posterize adjustment layer above the image: 4 levels. Ran; it sits on top and so flattens the result of the Cutout step below as well.

Filter > Artistic > Cutout on the image layer (target 'photo'): No. of Levels 5, Edge Simplicity 4, Edge Fidelity 2. Ran. The run shows the picture rebuilt from a few flat colours with roughly cut edges; the test bars at the bottom flatten into blocks too.

steps.name: Add Noise
steps.note: Filter > Noise > Add Noise on the image layer: 3 %, uniform, monochromatic. Ran; a faint ink texture. Untested: tracing the result to vector for real separations (manual).
history: New Posterize Layer; active layer: Posterize 1
history: Cutout; active layer: Background
history: Add Noise; active layer: Background

verified.note: Picture reduced to a handful of flat ink colours (about eight cover most of the frame) with roughly cut shapes; reads as a gig-poster screen print, though the subjects merge into the olive background.

steps.note: On the placed photo: Image Trace with a 4-6 colour preset and expand it into flat filled shapes (object model: placedItem.trace(), then tracing.expandTracing(); set the colour count in the Image Trace panel).
A very small corner roughen on the traced group makes the edges look cut by hand (verified: sharp irregular teeth at 12 pt; here 1.5 pt).
Posterize with 4 levels. Run: the page changed by 19.21 on average (0-255). The picture is flat bands of colour.

cards.name: Comic book ink and dots
cards.summary: A photo turned into comic art: flat posterised colour, dark ink lines along the contrast edges and a dot screen showing in the shadows.
avoid: low-contrast or soft photos: the edge lines come out patchy; add contrast first
serious or sensitive news photos: the cartoon look trivialises them

steps.note: Layer > Duplicate Layer: ran, 'Background copy' (labelled 'top') is active; the original below becomes the ink layer.
Filter > Artistic > Poster Edges on the bottom copy (target 'photo'): Edge Thickness 3, Edge Intensity 4, Posterization 3. Ran; flat posterised tones with dark outlines along the edges.
Filter > Pixelate > Color Halftone on the top copy (target 'top'): Radius 6, angles 108 / 162 / 90 / 45. Ran; a fine dot screen.

Top copy set to Multiply at 40 % opacity (script: blend mode and layer opacity in one call): ran. The run shows flat posterised colour, dark ink lines along the contrast edges and a dot screen showing in the shadows. Untested: a soft or low-contrast photo (the recipe says add contrast first).

cards.name: Grunge distressed print
cards.summary: Artwork or type looks worn: ragged sprayed edges, speckled ink drop-outs and a rough surface grain, like a weathered poster or a well-used stamp.
avoid: corporate and clean-tech layouts
small text: drop-outs make it unreadable; distress only display sizes
print files that need crisp vector edges: the effect is raster

steps.note: Layer > Rasterize > Type on the type layer (input: 'GRUNGE' in Arial Black 330 px, #1E1E1E on a #E4DCCB paper ground): ran, the type is now pixels.

Layer > Flatten Image (new step): ran. The recipe allows working on a flattened copy; this is needed because Spatter only roughened the type's own colour, not the transparent edge of a rasterised layer (the first run left the letter edges clean), while on the flattened picture the letter edge meets the paper colour and goes ragged.
Filter > Brush Strokes > Spatter: Spray Radius 12, Smoothness 5. Ran. The run shows ragged, sprayed letter edges.

Script (new step, after Spatter): two ink drop-out layers, each made from grey filled with Add Noise (400 %, Gaussian, monochromatic), blurred (6 px for blotches, 1.2 px for specks), Auto Levels and Threshold (192 / 205), recoloured black to black and white to the paper colour #E4DCCB with a Gradient Map merged into it, and set to Lighten: only the paper-coloured spots show, painting paper colour over the ink. The flattened image is then flattened again. Ran. The first run had no drop-outs (the Grain step alone only roughened the ink). The run shows paper-coloured flecks and blotches in the letters.

steps.name: Grain
steps.note: Filter > Texture > Grain: Intensity 40, Contrast 60, Speckle. Ran; a fine speckle over letters and paper (it darkens rather than drops out ink; the drop-outs come from the step above).

steps.name: Texturizer
steps.note: Filter > Texture > Texturizer: Sandstone, Scaling 100, Relief 6, light from the top left. Ran; a rough sandstone-like surface grain over letters and paper. Untested: a scanned paper or wall texture in Multiply, which gives the most convincing grunge (your own scan, manual).

Effect > Brush Strokes > Spatter: sprayed, ragged edges. Illustrator runs Photoshop Effects as raster effects at Document Raster Effects Settings resolution: set 300 ppi for print first.
Effect > Texture > Grain, speckle, for drop-outs.

sr = app.CreateShapeRange()
for k in ("orange_box", "blue_star", "grad_circle", "pgd_type", "zigzag"):

steps.note: Setup (script): the five vector plate shapes are grouped and flattened with ConvertToBitmapEx (RGB, 96 dpi, white background) so bitmap effects can act on them.

Scatter, 16 px both ways, on the flattened art: pixels near every edge are thrown a few pixels in random directions, so the clean edges of the star, box, circle and letters turn ragged and sprayed (the recipe's spatter edge).
Add Noise on the art: Gaussian, level 30, density 60: a rough surface grain over the ink.

steps.script:
art = s
r = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
r.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#808080"))
r.Outline.SetNoOutline()
labels["mask"] = r.ConvertToBitmapEx(4, False, False, 20)
labels["art"] = art
result = labels["mask"]
steps.note: Drop-out mask, step 1 (script): a page-size mid-grey rectangle is flattened to a coarse bitmap (RGB, 20 dpi, 400 x 225 px, so its specks are about 5 px of the page); the next steps turn it into a blotchy black-and-white speckle pattern.
Add Noise on the grey bitmap: Gaussian, level 100, density 100: random light and dark pixels.

Gaussian Blur, radius 20, on the noise: meant to clump the random pixels into blotches; on this 20 dpi bitmap it barely does (the judged frame: the specks stay small and even, about 4 px of the page), so the drop-outs read as uniform speckle, not worn patches. A larger radius or a lower dpi would give blotches (untested).
Light effect: contrast +100 and brightness -35: the soft blotches are pushed apart into dark and light areas.
Posterize with 2 levels: every pixel becomes pure black or pure white, a blotchy speckle mask.

steps.script:
s.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
s.Transparency.MergeMode = 28
result = s
steps.note: Drop-outs on the art (script): the speckle bitmap is set to Screen (Transparency.MergeMode 28) over the art, so its black leaves the ink alone and each white speck bleaches the ink under it to white: speckled ink drop-outs.
script ran
ApplyBitmapEffect('ScatterEffect Horizontal=16,Vertical=16,Square=1')

cards.name: Printed-on-paper texture
cards.summary: Flat digital artwork picks up the feel of uncoated paper or canvas: a fine embossed tooth, a slight warm tone and soft grain.
use_for: illustrations and posters that feel too digital
avoid: UI and screen graphics that must stay crisp
large relief values: the texture overpowers the art
CorelDRAW Wave Paper when colours must hold: its render faded colours strongly toward pastel

steps.note: Layer > Flatten Image (new first step, input: 'PAPER' in Arial Black 330 px, #F5E9D0 on a #2F6F8F ground): ran, the flat artwork is one layer so the texture covers type and ground alike.
Filter > Texture > Texturizer: Canvas, Scaling 100, Relief 4, light from the top left. Ran. The run shows a fine woven tooth over the whole frame, subtle at 960 px, colours kept.
Photo Filter adjustment layer: #E8C9A0, Density 15, Preserve Luminosity on. Ran; a slight warm paper cast.

steps.name: Add Noise
steps.note: Filter > Noise > Add Noise on the flattened layer (target 'background'): 2 %, Gaussian, monochromatic. Ran; fine fibre grain. Untested: other relief values and a real paper scan (manual).

verified.note: Fine canvas tooth over the whole frame, a slight warm shift in the ground and soft grain, with the colours and type kept.

steps.note: Effect > Texture > Texturizer, canvas, light top left, on the artwork group. Illustrator runs Photoshop Effects as raster effects at Document Raster Effects Settings resolution: set 300 ppi for print first.

steps.script:
r = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
r.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#808080"))
r.Outline.SetNoOutline()
labels["tooth"] = r.ConvertToBitmapEx(4, False, False, 96)
result = labels["tooth"]
steps.note: Setup (script): a page-size mid-grey rectangle is flattened to a bitmap (RGB, 96 dpi, 1920 x 1080 px): the blank sheet the paper tooth is made on. No paper scan ships with PGD, so the tooth is made from noise.
Add Noise on the grey sheet: Gaussian, level 80, density 100: random light and dark specks, the raw grain of the paper.
Gaussian Blur, radius 12: the specks soften into fibres.
Emboss on the sheet, depth 6, level 80, light from 135 degrees: the soft grain becomes a fine relief with light and dark edges, an embossed tooth.

steps.script:
s.StretchEx(PW / 2, PH / 2, 1.02, 1.02)
s.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(45)
s.Transparency.MergeMode = 29

warm.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#F0DDB8"))
warm.Outline.SetNoOutline()
warm.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(72)
warm.Transparency.MergeMode = 9
result = s
steps.note: Paper on the art (script): the tooth sheet is scaled 2 percent so the embossed edge of its own border leaves the page, then set to Overlay at 55 percent opacity (Transparency.MergeMode 29, transparency 45): the relief shows clearly on the mid-tone ground and only faintly on the light type (Overlay barely changes near-white; judged pixel spread about 1 on the type against 5 on the ground), and the colours stay; a warm rectangle (#F0DDB8) in Multiply at 28 percent opacity adds the slight warm paper cast (the recipe's Photo Filter layer).

verified.note: Fixed: a fine embossed tooth and soft grain now show clearly over the blue ground and the colours hold (no beige wash); the type warms slightly. The tooth is much weaker on the light type than on the ground (pixel spread about 1 vs 5), contrary to the step note.

manual_steps: Supply your own paper scan for the CorelDRAW bitmap-pattern transparency (no texture file ships with PGD).

cards.name: Torn-paper collage piece
cards.summary: A photo or colour block sits on a scrap of paper with a ragged torn edge and a soft shadow, ready to layer into a collage.
avoid: perfectly repeating edges: tear each piece with a new random seed or the collage looks stamped
tiny pieces: a torn edge needs at least 300 px to read

steps.note: On a white or paper-coloured rectangle: corner points, fine detail, a few points of size: a jagged torn edge (verified: sharp irregular teeth).
Soft shadow right and down so the scrap lifts off the page (verified: shadow offset right / down for positive values).
For a photo scrap: a second roughened shape over the photo, both selected, Make Clipping Mask.

steps.script:
bg = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
bg.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#CDBFA5"))
bg.Outline.SetNoOutline()
bg.OrderToBack()

sc_.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#FFFFFF"))
sc_.Outline.SetNoOutline()
result = sc_
steps.note: Setup (script): a kraft-coloured backdrop and a white rectangle 9.5 x 5.34 in for the paper scrap.
Zipper distortion on the paper scrap (amplitude 6, frequency 30, Random on, Smooth off): an irregular torn edge.

s.ConvertToCurves()
result = s
steps.note: Convert to Curves bakes the torn edge into the shape so a PowerClip can use it.

ph.SetSize(9.5, 5.34)
ph.CenterX, ph.CenterY = PW / 2, PH / 2
ph.AddToPowerClip(s, 0)
result = s

cards.name: Woodcut / linocut print
cards.summary: A photo becomes a bold two-tone relief print: solid black ink shapes with carved, slightly rough edges on paper.
avoid: busy, low-contrast photos: the two-tone cut loses the subject; pick a strong silhouette
fine facial detail: it fills in; crop tighter

cards.name: Line engraving
cards.summary: A photo rendered as fine engraved lines whose thickness follows the tone, the banknote / old-print engraving look.
use_for: editorial illustrations with a classic print feel
avoid: small output: the lines merge into grey; keep the line count low for small sizes
screens with scaling: line screens moire when resized; export at final size

steps.note: Filter > Sketch > Halftone Pattern: Size 2, Contrast 10, Line. Ran: black-and-white horizontal lines that thicken in the shadows and thin out in the highlights, with the picture still readable. The recipe's Graphic Pen step is an alternative to this one, not a second pass: run on top of it in the first run it replaced the clean lines with broken, noisy scratches, so the plan now runs the one line screen only. Untested: the line count at small sizes and moire after resizing; the lines are straight, not curved to the form as in a banknote engraving.
history: Halftone Pattern; active layer: Background

verified.note: Graphic Pen no longer overwrites the line screen and line weight follows tone (the dark share per block tracks the input tone, r = -0.98), but at 1:1 the lines are soft grey waves, not clean engraved strokes: about 42 % of photo pixels are mid-grey and the gaps in the shadows only reach grey 110, so it reads as a scan-line screen over a black-and-white photo.

steps.note: On the placed photo: Effect > Sketch > Graphic Pen. Illustrator runs Photoshop Effects as raster effects at Document Raster Effects Settings resolution: set 300 ppi for print first.

steps.script:
s.Bitmap.ConvertTo(2)
result = s
steps.note: Convert the photo to grayscale (Bitmap.ConvertTo(2)): the tones the lines will follow.
Light effect on the greyscale photo: contrast +20, brightness +22, so the lines run from fine in the lights to heavy in the darks instead of filling the dark picture solid.

steps.note: Line screen (script): Bitmap.ConvertToBW with the Halftone render type (5) and the Line halftone (2), angle 45 degrees, size 16, the 1-bit conversion CorelDRAW offers under Bitmaps > Mode > Black and White: the photo becomes diagonal black lines whose thickness follows the tone, the engraving look. The Pen & Ink effect of the first run only gave a grainy stipple at this size.

steps.script:
ink = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
ink.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#1B2A4A"))
ink.Outline.SetNoOutline()
ink.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
ink.Transparency.MergeMode = 11
paper = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
paper.Fill.ApplyUniformFill(rgb("#F3EAD3"))
paper.Outline.SetNoOutline()
paper.Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(0)
paper.Transparency.MergeMode = 9

steps.note: Ink and paper (script): a deep blue-black rectangle (#1B2A4A) in If Lighter mode is meant to turn the black lines into that ink, and a warm paper rectangle (#F3EAD3) in Multiply turns the white into paper. In the judged frame only the paper tone shows: the lines stay the same warm near-black as before this step (the Multiply paper layer darkens the ink back), so the ink colour is not achieved; colouring the 1-bit bitmap's black (or the ink rectangle above the paper) is the untested fix.
